6af55eec808d34e7ad17f788.one_liner: HSBC's Asia panel debates the dollar/Fed backdrop and the AI capex financing story (hyperscalers turning free-cash-flow negative, debt/equity raising, vendor-financing circularity) -- rates/dollar and financing-adjacent, but mostly an equity/tech-hardware conversation rather than money-market or credit-market content.
6af55eec808d34e7ad17f788.recap: HSBC's Under the Banyan Tree panel (Fred Newman, Harold, FX strategist Paul Mackel, tech analyst Frank, and auto/hardware analyst Yuchen) discuss the recent equity pullback, driven by inflation/oil worries, rising bond yields on Fed tightening expectations, and an AI valuation shakeout. Mackel argues the dollar remains supported by Fed rate signaling and strong equity-driven capital inflows into the US, sees recurring de-dollarization fears as overdone, flags the RMB as a long-running outperformer since September 2024, expects yen weakness to fade slowly given the US-Japan rate differential, and notes gold has actually fallen this year despite high macro risk, though he stays structurally long-term bullish on it. Frank covers AI hardware: hyperscaler capex is seen rising from $750bn this year to roughly $1.5tn next year, the first year these firms turn free-cash-flow negative and must raise debt or equity, pushing net debt/equity to a still-manageable 15-20%; he flags vendor-financing circularity (chipmakers funding customers who buy their chips) as a reason valuations stay capped despite near-100% margins, alongside power/data-center buildout delays as a newer risk, while underlying GPU demand (via rental pricing) still looks firm. Yuchen discusses autonomous driving's readiness being gated by regulation rather than technology, and argues China's AI buildout runs at a fraction of US capex, optimizing efficiency under export-control constraints rather than frontier scale, with real China-US hardware overlap concentrated in optical components (China ~70% of that market), prompting US diversification efforts.
